newsitem.title: UK: British consumers seen set for Christmas sales surge.
newsitem.headline: British consumers seen set for Christmas sales surge.

text.p: Spending on Britain's high streets has been subdued in recent weeks, even though Christmas is approaching, but industry analysts say the festive season will prompt a surge in sales which may prove enduring.

The British Retail Consortium's latest survey showed retail sales growth slowed in November to its lowest rate for seven months. Like-for-like retail sales grew 4.9 percent year-on-year in value in November, down from 5.9 in October.
The BRC said that slowdown reinforced its view that a re-run of the 1980s boom was not on the cards.

Last week, the Confederation of British Industry's distributive trades survey painted a similar picture. The balance of firms reporting higher sales than at the same point a year ago dipped to 48 percent from 55 in October.
But Christmas is coming and if gifts were not bought in November, they should be purchased much more rapidly this month, the analysts said.

The CBI said it expected consumers to start spending more in December. And independent consultants Verdict predict a 7.7 percent increase in spending this month over last December. That translates into about an extra 20 billion pounds ($32.9 billion) pouring into shop tills.
John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International, said consumers might have held back ahead of Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's November 26 budget.
"Now, consumers have got tax cuts, a rising housing market, falling unemployment and interest rates are not going up as quickly as thought. All the evidence adds up to a bumper Christmas," he said.

Andrew Sentance, director of the Centre for Economic Forecasting at the London Business School, said sales volumes would be around four percent higher in December than they were last December, while values could rise by about six percent.
"That's healthy growth but not accelerating out of control." He said consumer spending would rise by about four percent next year.

One reason why a traditional, festive mini-boom might prove to be much longer-lasting, stretching through next year, is that a tidal wave of cash will wash into consumers' pockets as tax-exempt savings deposits (TESSAs) mature and windfall payments from building society mergers and flotations are paid.

Many economists expect most of that cash to be reinvested in savings schemes. But after years of counting the pennies, will the average British consumer be able to resist the temptation to spend, spend, spend?
"This is one of the big uncertainties," Sentance said. "Economic theory suggests windfalls are saved but we know people have been cash-constrained and so might wish to spend."

Rob Thomas, building societies analyst at UBS, said the Bristol and West Building Society will pay out 600 million pounds in cash while the Halifax, Woolwich, Alliance & Leicester and Northern Rock Building Societies will offer shares to members worth 10, three, 2.5 and one billion pounds, respectively.
That adds up to a grand total of about 17 billion pounds.

"Even if only 20 percent was spent, that's an extra three billion pounds plus in the economy next year," Thomas said. "Also, these flotations are likely to take place over the summer so we'll see a sudden increase in people's wealth."

That sharp surge in spending around the middle of the year could stoke the inflationary fires and force the government to abandon its assumption that its 2.5 percent target for underlying inflation will be met.
Already, retail price inflation excluding mortgage interest payments is running at 3.3 percent year-on-year.
"All of this indicates there might be some early rebuilding of price margins by retailers," Shepperd said. "In the coming year, they will certainly have the opportunity to try."
